topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A report first copies every even reading into a temporary vector and then copies their squares into another vector. A range pipeline can describe the same selection and transformation without materializing both intermediate collections. But the pipeline borrows its source, so returning it after the source dies would be a lifetime defect.

blocks.text: A pipeline can look like a finished collection while being only a recipe for visiting another collection. That distinction is the central lesson of ranges and views. HarborWorks filters unfinished tasks and transforms them into report rows. The recipe may borrow the task vector, hold a predicate, and compute text only when traversed. Copying that recipe need not copy any tasks or precompute any rows.

blocks.text: The pipeline is useful because it exposes the sequence of operations. It is dangerous when its attractive notation hides ownership, invalidation, or repeated work. Before returning a view, ask what it refers to, what its callable captures, how long each dependency lives, and which mutations are allowed between construction and traversal. A view is not automatically a snapshot, a cache, or a safe asynchronous message.

topics.title: 18.1.1 Treating Sequences as Range Objects
topics.summary: Treating a sequence as a range lets an algorithm express what it traverses without hard-coding one container. It still needs capabilities such as input traversal or random access depending on the operation. C++20 concepts make many of those requirements visible in algorithm interfaces.

Destroying a lightweight view object does not necessarily destroy the source, while keeping a view object alive does not necessarily keep borrowed source storage alive. blocks.text: A range supplies a way to obtain a beginning and an end under the range requirements. The two endpoints need not have the same type; an iterator and a sentinel can cooperate to describe termination. The abstraction includes standard containers, arrays, spans, and adapted sequences, but their ownership and traversal properties differ. “It is a range” is the start of an analysis, not a complete description.

blocks.text: A vector owns its elements. A span describes a contiguous sequence owned elsewhere. A filtering view may own a lightweight wrapper that refers to another range. A generating range can compute values rather than store a conventional array of them. Algorithms can operate through the common interface, but callers still need to know whether traversal is single-pass, multipass, random access, sized, contiguous, or borrowed.

blocks.text: A range being sized does not imply contiguous storage, and random access does not imply one contiguous allocation. Conversely, a range can be useful without knowing its size cheaply. Avoid adding a preliminary distance calculation to every pipeline merely to reserve output space. With some ranges, that calculation can consume work or require an extra traversal. Select the allocation strategy from the actual range category and workload.

blocks.text: The borrowed-range concept concerns whether iterators can remain usable after the range object itself is destroyed. It does not promise that the elements live forever. A temporary span over a live array can yield a usable iterator because the span does not own the array. The same span over storage that is about to disappear cannot manufacture a longer element lifetime. Distinguish the lifetime of the wrapper from the lifetime of the data.

blocks.text: Range algorithms use return types such as std::ranges::dangling to prevent certain unsafe results from temporary non-borrowed ranges. This is a useful compile-time boundary, not a complete lifetime checker. A view can still refer to an already-dead owner through an incorrectly constructed reference. The supplemental range-lifetime lab demonstrates safe compile-time distinctions without dereferencing a dangling object.

blocks.text: A projection is not a promise of free computation or cached results. If extracting a key is expensive, its repeated evaluation may matter. Choose a representation or precomputed key strategy only after profiling a real workload. Range syntax makes an interface concise; it does not eliminate the algorithm’s complexity or semantic ordering requirements.

Choose a representation or precomputed key strategy only after profiling a real workload. Range syntax makes an interface concise; it does not eliminate the algorithm’s complexity or semantic ordering requirements.

blocks.text: Range-based algorithms accept a range directly and often support projections, reducing boilerplate around begin/end pairs and member extraction. A projection selects the value to compare without requiring the comparator to know the entire record. Sorting tasks by a tuple projection can make a deterministic priority-and-ID contract explicit. The projection must still return values whose comparison satisfies the algorithm’s requirements.
rich: Range-based algorithms accept a range directly and often support projections, reducing boilerplate around begin/end pairs and member extraction. A projection selects the value to compare without requiring the comparator to know the entire record. Sorting tasks by a tuple projection can make a deterministic priority-and-ID contract explicit. The projection must still return values whose comparison satisfies the algorithm’s requirements.

blocks.text: A shorter call does not change invalidation rules or ownership. Sorting a vector through a ranges algorithm mutates the vector just as the corresponding iterator-based operation does. Finding an element returns a position whose continued use depends on the owner. Passing a temporary owning range can change the safe return type. Read the result type as carefully as the call expression.

blocks.text: Concept-based diagnostics can identify that a range lacks random-access capability or that a comparator cannot be invoked with the projected values. They cannot generally prove that the comparator establishes a strict weak ordering over every possible value. They also cannot prove that a borrowed source will remain alive during later execution. Compile-time constraints remove some invalid programs; semantic review handles obligations the type system does not express.

blocks.text: The language baseline for this book is C++20. Later standards add convenient range facilities, but a compiler accepting C++20 does not promise those additions. The worked program materializes a view with an explicit loop rather than depending on a later conversion helper. That choice keeps the example’s portability claim narrow and makes the construction of owned output visible.

topics.summary: The filter view examines source elements and yields those satisfying the even predicate. It does not create a new owning vector of selected integers. blocks.text: Some views cache traversal state. Mutating a source in ways that invalidate iterators or change predicate-relevant structure can make reuse subtle or invalid. The example rebuilds its filter after changing the source rather than presenting a view as an automatically maintained database query. For a stable snapshot, materialize an owning result at a deliberate boundary.

blocks.text: A filtering view selects elements during traversal according to a predicate. Constructing the view does not normally create a second container containing only the matches. Its iterators find qualifying positions in the underlying range. This saves an intermediate copy, but it also means later traversal depends on the underlying elements and the predicate’s retained state.

blocks.text: A captured threshold illustrates the timing. Capturing an integer threshold by value stores the chosen value in the callable. Capturing it by reference makes later traversal depend on the current external integer and its lifetime. Both forms can be correct; they express different contracts. A pipeline sent to another component should not unexpectedly depend on a local threshold that has already gone out of scope.

blocks.text: Filtering may cache traversal state to meet its complexity requirements. In particular, a filter over a forward range can cache a beginning position. Changing source elements after a view has been used does not mean every future operation recomputes from the original first element. The teaching rule is to keep a view within a period of stable source state and reconstruct the view after a mutation that changes membership assumptions.

blocks.text: Even preserving storage addresses does not make every filtered mutation safe. The iterator and adaptor contracts restrict operations that would undermine their assumptions about selected elements. Do not use a filter over positive values and casually mutate the currently selected values so they no longer satisfy the predicate while assuming the same traversal remains valid. For an update, first identify stable targets or construct a separate result, then perform a reviewed mutation.

blocks.text: A transform view computes its output as elements are accessed. Repeated traversal can repeat the computation. A transform that parses text, allocates strings, or queries external state therefore has observable work beyond the apparent simplicity of the pipeline expression. A view is not memoization. If repeated processing should use a stable result, materialize an owning collection at the appropriate boundary.

blocks.text: Returning references from a transform requires special care. Returning a reference to the current source element can be reasonable while the source remains valid. Returning a reference to a local temporary created inside the callable is not. Returning a string view into a temporary formatted string is equally unsafe despite the absence of an explicit reference symbol. Trace the owner of the returned bytes, not merely the type’s spelling.

blocks.text: Adaptor order affects both meaning and work. Filtering records before formatting them can avoid formatting rejected records. Transforming first and then filtering formatted strings applies the predicate to a different domain and can allocate for every input. The operations commute only when their semantics justify that transformation. Do not reorder pipelines based solely on an intuition that filters should always come first.

blocks.text: Side effects make lazy evaluation harder to reason about. A predicate that increments a counter may be called more often than a casual reader expects as iterators advance or new traversals begin. A formatter that writes to a log on every dereference can produce duplicate entries. Prefer pure selection and transformation functions in ordinary views. When effects are required, use an explicit eager loop whose execution count and failure boundary are clear.

blocks.text: The final materialization point is an ownership decision. An owning vector of report rows can outlive the input, travel to another layer, and remain unchanged when the source is edited. It consumes storage and construction work, but buys a clear contract. The best design is not the one with the fewest allocations in isolation; it is the one that pays for ownership where independent lifetime is actually needed.

topics.title: Failure clinic — A returned pipeline that borrows a dead vector
topics.summary: A function creates a local vector, builds a filter over it, and returns the filter. The returned type may be perfectly well formed. The function still destroys its local vector on return, leaving the recipe without a valid source. Storing the returned view in a variable does not restore the destroyed elements. The appropriate repair is an owning result or a deliberately owning range arrangement whose dependencies are all valid.

Test empty input, no matches, all matches, and multiple priority groups. For the owning version, change or destroy the original input after the function returns and verify that the rows remain unchanged. For the borrowed version, keep all dependencies alive and unchanged throughout consumption; do not manufacture an invalid test merely to hope that a sanitizer catches it.

Count formatting calls in a controlled experiment to show the difference between constructing a lazy recipe and materializing its result. Treat the counter as instrumentation, not as a promised universal call count for every adaptor implementation. Explain why repeating a traversal can repeat formatting and why a cached output vector behaves differently.

topics.summary: Ranges unify traversal interfaces; they do not unify ownership. Views often defer work and can retain borrows. Borrowed-range properties do not prolong the lifetime of external storage. Reconstructing views after relevant source changes is a clear teaching discipline.
